description: The roc, called rukh in Persian, is a colossal bird of prey from the tales of One Thousand and One Nights. With wings that blot out the sun and talons large enough to lift an elephant, it carries its prey to mountain-top nests. In the voyages of Sinbad the Sailor, sailors mistake its egg for a dome, and the furious bird hurls stones at ships that break it.
source: Wikipedia: Roc (mythology); One Thousand and One Nights
research_notes: The roc is attested across Arabic and Persian sources; the English roc descends from Arabic rukhkh, itself from Persian rukh. Its nest is placed in the Valley of Diamonds and on the island of Waqwaq. Wittkower traced the bird's origin to the Indian Garuda, who battles the Naga serpent, while others connect it to the pre-Islamic anqa, a giant human-faced bird with four wings.

description: The ghoul is a flesh-eating desert demon of Arab and Jordanian folklore, classed among the diabolical jinn and said to be offspring of Iblis. It haunts graveyards, ruins, and empty wastes, shifting shape freely but betrayed by its unalterable ass's hooves. Usually female, it lures travellers as an old woman or lost relative, then devours them; a single blow kills it, a second restores it to life.
source: Britannica: Ghoul; Encyclopaedia Iranica s.v. Gul; Wikipedia
research_notes: Belief in the ghoul predates Islam and appears in pre-Islamic poetry such as Ta'abatta Sharran's famous encounter. Al-Qazwini records that demons struck by comets while eavesdropping on heaven fell to earth and became ghuls. In Jordanian folktales the ghoul often appears as an old woman tricking children and travellers. Iron, salt, and Quranic verses are said to repel it.

description: Not independently attested in Yemeni folklore under this name. Sayad is described as a female jinn, tall with long hair, sagging breasts, and donkey legs, who manifests through those who fear her and seizes possession. The figure closely resembles Umm al-Subyan, the child-stealing night demon of South Arabia, and may be a mislabeled variant of that attested being.
source: Yemeni oral tradition (nominal); cf. Umm al-Subyan accounts (W.H. Ingrams)
research_notes: No independent source names a Yemeni jinn Sayad. The description matches Umm al-Subyan, the child-stealing night spirit of South Arabia documented by travellers such as W.H. Ingrams. The donkey legs echo the classic ghul's tell-tale hooves. The figure is best treated as an unattested regional variant.

description: The si'lat is a shape-shifting female jinn of Palestinian and wider Arab folklore, kin to the ghoul but wickeder and unable to change her limbs. She lurks in abandoned wells, deep caves, and wasteland, appearing as a seductive woman to lure men to their ruin. Those who answer her falsely are lost, while truth-telling and invoking God may break her hold.
source: Wikipedia: Si'la; Palestinian oral tradition
research_notes: The si'la (plural sa'ali) is attested in medieval Arabic sources; unlike the mutable ghoul she is described as immutable in shape. Lane's lexicon glosses her as a witchlike species of jinn. In Palestine the si'lat is tied to wells and caves and to the danger of superficial beauty.

description: The jann are the primordial fire-born jinn of pre-Islamic Arabia, created from smokeless flame before the coming of Islam. They haunt desert paths and oases, appearing to travellers as whirlwinds of sand or as a beautiful white camel that leads them astray. Capable of every shape, they are as likely to help as to harm, their root name meaning to conceal.
source: Encyclopaedia Iranica s.v. Genie; Qur'an 55:14
research_notes: The Qur'an states the jinn were created from smokeless fire (55:14), and a whole sura is named for them. The root janna means to conceal. In Arab and Persian lore the jann are reckoned the earliest and most primitive class of jinn, and their whirlwind and white-camel guises are stock motifs of desert traveller tales.

description: The jinn of Jordan are fire-born spirits, created of smokeless flame, who dwell in abandoned houses, wells, deep caves, and desert wastes. They can take any form and possess the unwary, yet they can be helpful as well as harmful. Jordanians speak of jinn dancing at crossroads and guard against them with prayer, iron, and the rule of never mentioning them at night.
source: Kufr Yuba fieldwork (J-Stage); Al-Momani (2025); Jarrah et al. (2026)
research_notes: Ethnographic fieldwork in Kufr Yuba, north Jordan, records jinn as a masculine singular living in wells and deserted houses, with tales of jinn dancing at the village crossroads. A famous Jordanian tale tells of a poor farmer enriched by a jinn whose fortune vanished when he broke his promise. Everyday speech uses apotropaic formulas because mentioning them brings them.

description: The ifrit is a powerful and malevolent class of jinn in Arab and Islamic tradition, famed for brute strength, cunning, and a rebellious nature. The Qur'an names the ifrit of the jinn who offered to carry the throne of Bilqis. In popular tales ifrits appear as enormous winged beings of fire and magic, bound to the underworld and to the spirits of the dead.
source: Britannica: Ifrit; Wikipedia
research_notes: The word ifrit, from the root afara meaning rebellious and strong, always appears in the Qur'an qualified by among the jinn (27:39). Medieval lore came to conflate the ifrit with the marid, another powerful jinn type. In story cycles ifrits are often imprisoned in vessels and forced to serve the heroes who master them.

description: The ifrit, spelled variously ifrit and afrit, is a mighty class of rebellious fire-jinn renowned for guile and supernatural power. It is first met in the Qur'anic tale of the throne of Sheba, where an ifrit of the jinn volunteers to bring it in an instant. Folk tradition pictures the ifrit as a towering winged being of smoke and flame dwelling in ruins and desolate wastes.
source: Britannica: Ifrit; One Thousand and One Nights
research_notes: Variant transliterations ifrit and afrit reflect the same Arabic figure, classed among the jinn and rooted in the triliteral afara meaning rebellious and strong. The Nights and Persian romance cycles feature ifrits as warrior-demon adversaries or bound servants. The Qur'anic ifrit of 27:39 is the earliest fixed reference.

description: The pari, or peri, is a Persian winged spirit of radiant beauty, born of fire yet gentle and luminous. Early Persian belief classed the paris among the evil spirits of the dark, but in Islamic-period lore they grew into benevolent beings who dwell in hidden, shimmering palaces and mingle with mortals in love and art. They stand in sharp contrast to the ugly, brutish divs.
source: Wikipedia: Pari; Encyclopaedia Iranica
research_notes: The Middle Persian term parig lies behind the modern pari; it appears in Iranian tradition as an ambivalent supernatural being, originally sinister and later idealized. The Persian word divanah, meaning mad, literally describes one who lost his wits for love of a pari. In Middle Persian literature comets were identified with paris.

description: The helpful fish of Qatari coastal lore is a benevolent water spirit that guards tide pools and the shallow Gulf waters, guiding honest fishermen to good catches. Often identified with the two-banded porgy known locally as al-fisaikra, it embodies foresight and clear speech, rewarding respect and punishing greed. Tales of the guide fish remain part of Gulf oral heritage.
source: Qatari oral tradition; Words Without Borders (Al Fisaikra)
research_notes: The helpful fish aligns with Qatari stories of the two-banded porgy, al-fisaikra, a fish of ritual and folk significance along the Gulf coast. It is linked in the database to other Gulf water spirits such as Bu Draeyah and Baba Dariah. As a household spirit it reflects pearl-diving communities' gratitude toward the sea.

description: Not independently attested in Turkish folklore under this name. Nisanci is described as a giant, fifteen to twenty feet tall with a long beard, who works at night shaping the hills and rock fields of Anatolia and hurls boulders at mockers. The tale echoes genuine Anatolian giant lore and the Ottoman court office of nisanci, but no documented folk being bears this name.
source: Turkish folklore (nominal); Ottoman court office of nisanci
research_notes: No accessible source independently attests a giant named Nisanci. The being echoes genuine Anatolian and Balkan tales of giants who shaped the land, threw stones, and built megaliths, while the title nisanci historically belongs to an Ottoman court office. The figure reads as an AI-minted amalgam of those motifs rather than a documented folk being.

description: Bu Draeyah is a giant sea serpent of Qatari legend, deep blue of scale with glowing golden eyes, who guards the pearl beds of the Persian Gulf. He is a water spirit of harsh judgement: generous to honest divers, destructive to the greedy who strip his reefs. Sacred chants are said to soothe him, and his name is still spoken in pearl-diving households.
source: Folklore Thursday: Qatari pearl-diving lore; Qatari oral tradition
research_notes: Bu Draeyah is attested in Qatari pearl-diving folklore as a protector of the oyster beds who punishes avarice. The tale encodes the real dangers of the old pearling economy and the ethics of taking only what is needed. Popular retellings match the record's deep blue scales and glowing gold eyes.

description: Baba Dariah, Father of the Tide, is a water jinn of Emirati tradition who rules the deep waters and coral reefs of the Gulf. He commands the tides and speaks to the creatures of the sea, shielding honest boatmen while dragging the arrogant to the depths. The Gulf coast still respects his power, and his legend warns against taking the sea for granted.
source: The National News (2009); Emirati oral tradition
research_notes: Baba Dariah, rendered Father of the Sea, is documented in Emirati reports as a djinn of the deep feared and honored by Gulf seafarers. His story belongs to the same pearl-diving complex as Bu Draeyah. A 2009 National News account popularized the name for a tide-god of the Emirates.

description: Not independently attested in Sudanese folklore under this name. Tay is described as a serpent-like water spirit of the Nile who blesses fishermen with good catches or drags the disrespectful beneath the water. The figure fits the documented river-spirit world of northern Sudan and Nubia, including the banat el Hur and the River Folk, but no source names a being called Tay.
source: J.W. Crowfoot, Angels of the Nile, Sudan Notes and Records 2 (1919)
research_notes: No source names a Nile spirit Tay. The figure fits Crowfoot's documented river-spirit world of northern Sudan and Nubia, including the banat el Hur and the daughter of the River Folk drawn from a fisherman's net. The record appears to generalize attested beings under an invented name. The serpent form echoes other Nilotic river guardians.

description: Thoth, the ibis-headed god of the moon, is the Egyptian lord of wisdom, writing, magic, and judgement. Scribe of the gods and arbitrator of their disputes, he stands beside Ra's solar barque and records the verdicts of the dead. His cult center was Hermopolis, and the Greeks identified him with Hermes; his name means he who is like the ibis.
source: Wikipedia: Thoth; Pyramid Texts and Book of the Dead
research_notes: Thoth appears throughout the Pyramid Texts and Book of the Dead as the wise mediator and divine scribe. Depicted with the head of an ibis or a baboon, his consort was Ma'at and his feminine counterpart Seshat. The Greeks equated him with Hermes, giving rise to the Hermetic corpus.

description: The ghoul of Tunisian folklore is a shape-shifting desert demon of the jinn, haunting ruins, cemeteries, and lonely roads. It appears as a beautiful woman or a hunched crone to waylay travellers, whose flesh it devours. Unlike the Western grave-robber, the Tunisian ghoul is above all a deceiver of the wilderness, warded off by iron and the name of God.
source: Britannica: Ghoul; A.K. Al-Rawi, Folklore 120 (2009)
research_notes: Al-Rawi's study of the Arabic ghoul traces its North African variants, where it remains a shapeshifting deceiver rather than a corpse-eater; the grave-robbing ghoul is a Western addition from Galland's translation. In Tunisian and Maghrebi tales it is a female fiend of the wasteland. The figure survives in children's cautionary tales across the region.

description: Anubis, the jackal-headed god of the necropolis, is the guardian of mummification and the guide of souls into the afterlife. He presides over the Weighing of the Heart, balancing each soul against the feather of Ma'at. Son of Osiris, he embalmed the first corpse and has since opened the way for the dead, his black jackal form pacing the desert tombs.
source: Egyptian mythology; Pyramid Texts and Book of the Dead
research_notes: Anubis, Inpu in Egyptian, is attested from the Old Kingdom onward as the god of embalming and protector of the dead. His jackal form derives from the scavengers of the desert edge. In the Book of the Dead he is He who is upon his mountain, overseer of the scales and the weighing of hearts.

description: Apep, the great serpent of chaos, is the eternal enemy of the sun god Ra in Egyptian mythology. Each night he coils in the underworld to swallow the solar barque, and each dawn Ra's crew, aided by Seth and the magic of Isis, repels him. Storms were read as his writhing, and his name, written with the cut-hieroglyph, was ritually destroyed.
source: Wikipedia: Apep; Book of Overthrowing Apep
research_notes: Apep, Apophis in Greek, is documented from the New Kingdom in the Book of Overthrowing Apep, read to shield the sun each morning. He dwells in the waters of Nun, the primordial deep, beyond the western horizon. His role as Ra's adversary makes him a paradigm of chaos opposing cosmic order.

description: Not independently attested in Algerian folklore. Maure the Briden is described as a sea goddess of the Mediterranean who commands storms and shelters coastal villages, a water spirit bound to the shore and offended by pollution of the sea. The garbled name suggests a modern invention conflating the classic siren type with the Amazigh rain rites of Anzar, whose bride ends drought.
source: Algerian folklore (nominal); cf. Amazigh Anzar rain-bride rite
research_notes: No Algerian source names a Maure the Briden. The garbled form suggests an AI-generated placeholder. Real Amazigh tradition includes the rain god Anzar and rites in which a bride is symbolically wed to end drought, a plausible origin for the briden element. The being is best classed as unattested.

description: The desert jinn of Libya are wandering fire-born spirits of the Sahara who appear to travellers as guides and lead them astray. Their most famous haunt is Kaf Ajnoun, the Cave of the Jinn near Ghat, a haunted rock fortress where jinn gather, sometimes seen as an uncatchable deer. The Tuareg hold that jinn fear iron, so a blade is carried even to weddings.
source: Libya Observer (Kaf Ajnoun); Temehu; Tuareg oral tradition
research_notes: The Cave of the Jinn, Kaf Ajnoun, also called Idinen or the Fortress of Ghosts, is a documented haunted site north of Ghat, avoided by local Tuareg. Beliefs include jinn appearing as uncaught deer, mysterious voices, and the jinn's dread of iron. Explorers such as Barth and Clapperton reported strange experiences there.

description: The Egyptian sphinx is a guardian of sacred ground, carved with the head of a king or god upon the body of a lion. From the Great Sphinx of Giza to the ram-headed criosphinxes lining temple avenues, it stood watch over tombs and processional ways. It embodies royal power, the horizon god Horemakhet, and the silent strength of the desert edge.
source: Wikipedia: Sphinx; Egyptian mythology
research_notes: Unlike the riddle-posing sphinx of Greece, the Egyptian sphinx is a protective figure: the Great Sphinx at Giza, carved from a single limestone outcrop, guards the pyramids and was linked to the sun god as Horemakhet. Ram-headed criosphinxes flank the Karnak avenue. Royal power and wisdom are its core symbols.

description: Jok is the all-embracing class of spirits in Acholi belief, covering ancestral shades, nature powers, and the supreme creator. It can strike with illness and misfortune, yet it also grants protection, healing, and prosperity, and is honoured through song. Every clan and place possesses its own jok, weaving the seen and unseen worlds into one order.
source: Wikipedia: Jok; Acholi oral tradition
research_notes: The term jok is attested among the Acholi and neighbouring Nilotic peoples as a comprehensive spiritual force, from the high god to localized nature and ancestral spirits. It accounts for both calamity and blessing. Cognates in Dinka and Shilluk shape related Nilotic cosmology.

description: The phoenix of Egypt is the immortal sun bird, born of the east, that dies in flame and rises renewed from its own ashes. It is linked to the bennu heron of Heliopolis, symbol of Ra and the rising sun, and to the cycle of death and rebirth that sustains all life. Ancient writers set its life span at many centuries.
source: Wikipedia: Phoenix; Herodotus, Histories II
research_notes: Herodotus describes the Egyptian bird that visits Heliopolis every five hundred years, bearing its parent in a ball of myrrh; later versions add the pyre and rebirth from ashes. The bennu heron was the solar bird of Ra at Heliopolis. The themes of rebirth and renewal match this documented cycle.

description: Piath is a colossal serpent of Dinka belief, dwelling in the waters of the White Nile and its tributaries. Part of a world of river beings that shape floods and fishing fortunes, it demands care from those who use the water. As a nature spirit it is feared and respected, its moods read in the river's rise and fall.
source: Godfrey Lienhardt, Divinity and Experience (1961)
research_notes: Lienhardt's ethnography documents Nilotic water divinities and river powers around the Dinka. The record describes piath as a colossal White Nile serpent, a class consistent with Lienhardt's accounts of river-associated divinities. Documentation is secondary and the exact name is thin, so attestation is rated fair.

description: The zuhri is a being of Moroccan belief, born of a human mother and a jinn father, who can see buried treasure beneath the earth. Marked by a slanting gaze, the zuhri is sought by treasure hunters, while the treasures themselves are said to strike the greedy dead. The belief is so potent that it has been invoked in real, violent crimes.
source: Wikipedia: Zuhri; Moroccan oral tradition
research_notes: The zuhri is attested in Moroccan lore as a human-jinn hybrid with x-ray sight for hidden treasure. Belief in zuhri treasure-seekers has been cited in Moroccan murder cases where victims were killed on suspicion of being zuhri. The term derives from the idea of noon-hour supernatural sight.

description: The zar is a class of possessing spirits in Sudan, Egypt, and the Horn of Africa, believed to seize people, most often women, causing illness, restlessness, and affliction. Each zar demands its own clothes, jewels, incense, and drumming, met through the healing ceremonies of the zar cult. Seven nations of zar spirits range from holy men to European officials.
source: Zar possession studies (University of Cologne); J. Boddy, Wombs and Alien Spirits
research_notes: The zar cult took its present shape in Sudan in the mid-nineteenth century amid Ottoman military ranks. Spirits are grouped into seven nations, from the Darawish and Pashawat to the Khawajat, or Europeans, and the Habbashi, or Ethiopians. Rituals escalate through levels called Coffee, Chairs, and Karamat, using jabana coffee gatherings.

description: Not independently attested in Sudanese folklore by this name. Nina is described as a Nubian fertility spirit who appears as a beautiful woman or as water itself, protecting mothers and children and honoured in naming ceremonies. The closest documented beings are the Nubian water angels, malayket al-bahr, and the banat el Hur of the Nile, spirits of river, birth, and household.
source: Sudanese folklore (nominal); F. El Guindi, Angels in the Nile (2006)
research_notes: No source names a Sudanese or Nubian spirit Nina. The record's traits match attested Nubian river spirits, including the malayket al-bahr, or water angels, documented by Fadwa El Guindi, and the banat el Hur of Crowfoot's 1919 account, which protect women and children around the Nile. The name appears to be an AI-generated placeholder.

description: Nyikang, son of Kang, is the semi-legendary founder and divine ancestor of the Shilluk people. Said to be born of a human father and a crocodile naiad, he crossed the White Nile into Shilluk country, established the kingship, and later vanished into the river. Shilluk kings are believed to inherit his spirit, tying every reign to his living memory.
source: Wikipedia: Nyikang; Shilluk oral tradition
research_notes: Nyikang's name means son of Kang; his mother Nyikaya was a half-woman, half-crocodile naiad. He bears the epithets of ancestor, father, sky, and cloud, and is tied to the cosmic doum palm. The Shilluk king is held to incarnate Nyikang's spirit, connecting historical claim and territorial legitimacy.

description: Not independently attested in Kyrgyz folklore by this name. Teke, the Turkic word for the ibex, is here described as a guardian spirit of mountain passes and high peaks who protects or misleads according to respect shown. The documented protector of wild game in Kyrgyz and Turkic hunting tradition is Kayberen, guardian of ibex, deer, and mountain herds.
source: Kyrgyz oral tradition (nominal); Kayberen studies (dergipark.org.tr)
research_notes: Two searches found no Kyrgyz spirit named teke; the term is the common Turkic word for the ibex or he-goat. The real protector of game animals in Kyrgyz and Turkic hunting culture is Kayberen, also written Kaiberen. The record's guardian of mountain passes appears to be a fabrication layered onto genuine ibex veneration.

description: Tengri is the supreme sky god of the Turkic peoples, the eternal blue sky whose worship long preceded Islam in Central Asia. Creator and sustainer above all spirits, he was honoured by shamans and steppe nomads with open-air rites on high ground. Kazakh reverence for Tengri still echoes in proverbs and in prayerful raising of the hands to the sky.
source: Tengrism; Serikbol Konadybai; Central Asian Turkic-Mongol religion
research_notes: Tengri is attested across Turkic and Mongol peoples as the sky-father and cosmic orderer. He receives no idol, honoured in open air. The record credits Kazakh scholar Serikbol Konadybai for documenting the Kazakh tradition. Tengri's cult resurged in modern Kazakhstan as a marker of steppe identity.

description: Not independently attested in Kazakh folklore. This figure is described as a turtle animal-spirit and guardian of the cliffs, tied to forests and the Central Asian wilderness, protecting the land and teaching strength. Kazakh tradition centres on the horse, the eagle, and the wolf rather than any turtle guardian, and no source documents such a being.
source: Generic regional survey (Radlov, Shirokogoroff, Potanin)
research_notes: The record's source is a generic regional survey array, a hallmark of AI-generated placeholders. No Kazakh or Turkic tradition features a turtle guardian of cliffs. The record appears invented for the batch, as with the related turtle-nature-spirit entry. Real Kazakh animal lore centers on the horse, the eagle, and the wolf.

description: Not independently attested in Kazakh folklore. This figure is described as a turtle nature-spirit and guardian of the caves, a patient keeper of stamina and animal friendship who protects the woodlands. No documented Kazakh tradition names a cave-guarding turtle spirit, and the being appears to be a fabricated pair with the turtle animal-spirit entry.
source: Generic regional survey (Radlov, Shirokogoroff, Potanin)
research_notes: As with its companion entry, this record rests on a generic citation and reads as template-generated. Kazakh nature-spirit lore, including the masters of mountains and waters, does not include turtles. Both turtle records should be treated as inventions until primary evidence appears.

description: The tulpar is the winged horse of Kazakh and Turkic legend, a loyal steed of epic heroes who flies faster than the wind and shuttles between earth and the spirit realm. Its wings are said to be invisible by day, appearing only in darkness. Two golden tulpars adorn the national emblem of Kazakhstan, symbols of freedom, speed, and the open sky.
source: Wikipedia: Tulpar; Turkic oral tradition
research_notes: The tulpar is attested across Turkic epics as a celestial or winged horse akin to the Greek Pegasus. The proverb that the horse is the wing of the Turk captures its cultural weight. Kazakhstan's state emblem features two winged tulpars, confirming its status as a national symbol.

description: Taytoru is the magical steed of Semetey in the Kyrgyz Epic of Manas, a sleek, fiery-eyed horse of supernatural speed and endurance. She carried Semetey from Bukhara across the mountains to the Talas valley so he could avenge his father Manas's death. Loyal and shrewd, she is the archetype of the epic hero's faithful mount.
source: Epic of Manas; Kyrgyz oral tradition
research_notes: Taytoru is documented in the Manas cycle as the horse of Semetey. Her journey from Bukhara to Talas for vengeance is a fixed episode of the epic. As a tay, or colt, with supernatural gifts, she belongs to the Kyrgyz class of magical steeds alongside Ak-Kula and the Kazakh tulpar.

description: Khormusta, king of the western heavens, is the supreme sky deity of Buryat Tengriism and father of the hero Abai Geser. A radiant warrior-king amid celestial hosts, he wages eternal war against the eastern gods of darkness. His scattering of the slain Atai Ulan's body, meant to prevent resurrection, instead seeded the demons that plague the world.
source: Wikipedia: Epic of King Gesar; Buryat Tengriism
research_notes: Khormusta, also Turmas, Hormust, and Khorbustu, heads the fifty-five western tengri of Buryat cosmology. His war with Atai Ulan of the eastern heavens opens the Geser epic cycle, and his son Abai Geser descends to earth to fight evil. The name derives from Iranian Ahura Mazda via Central Asian transmission.
